q.q: When should implementation be planned?
o: While the new system is still being developed
Only after the post-implementation review
After the old system has been switched off
During the feasibility study only
q.why: Resources such as hardware and training take time to arrange.

q.q: Which task is part of implementation rather than design?
o: Producing the data dictionary for the fields
Storyboarding the screens and navigation
Writing the requirements specification
Converting existing records into the new system
q.why: Data conversion happens when the system goes live.

q.q: Which describes the purpose of implementation?
o: To decide what the new system should do for its users
To fix bugs that are discovered after the system goes live
To write and unit test the program code for each module
To put the new system into operation in place of the old one
q.why: Implementation makes the new system operational with minimal disruption and risk.

q.q: Why must implementation be planned during development rather than once the system is finished?
o: Implementation tasks can only be carried out while programmers are still writing code
Planning implementation early removes the need to carry out acceptance testing
The client is not allowed to see the system until implementation planning is complete
Some tasks, such as ordering hardware or releasing staff for training, take weeks to arrange
q.why: Many resources must be in place before the new system can take over.

q.q: Setting up user accounts, access levels and backups is part of which implementation task?
o: Installing and configuring software
Installing hardware and networks
Training
Data conversion
q.why: Configuring software includes accounts, access levels and backups.

q.q: What happens at handover, the final implementation task?
o: Before acceptance testing, the developer installs the hardware and the network
After the feasibility report, management decides to fund the project
After acceptance and sign-off, support begins and the system enters maintenance
During design, the client approves the screen layouts and storyboards
q.why: Handover follows sign-off and marks the move into maintenance.

q.q: Which pair of documentation types is provided during implementation?
o: Requirements specifications and data flow diagrams
Feasibility reports for managers and storyboards for users
Test plans for testers and storyboards for designers
User guides for staff and technical documentation for maintainers
q.why: Implementation supplies user and technical documentation.

q.q: A new system may replace which of these?
o: Only a paper-based system, never a computer one
Either an older computer system or a paper-based one
Only an older computer system, never a paper one
Only a system built by the same developer
q.why: Implementation replaces whatever was used before, computer or paper.

q.q: Which phrase best describes the aim of implementation?
o: Complete implementation as quickly as possible regardless of disruption
Make the new system fully operational with as little disruption and risk as possible
Run the old system for as long as possible before the new one is introduced
Make the new system as cheap as possible regardless of risk to the organisation
q.why: The purpose is full operation with minimal disruption and risk.

q.q: Which list contains only implementation tasks?
o: Draw storyboards, build prototypes, write the data dictionary
Interview staff, draw DFDs, write the specification, sign off
Unit test, integration test, system test, beta test
Install hardware, convert data, train staff, choose a changeover method
q.why: The others are analysis, design and testing tasks respectively.

q.q: Which changeover method has the highest risk?
o: Parallel
Phased
Direct
Pilot
q.why: With no overlap, failure leaves nothing to fall back on.

q.q: A chain of pharmacies introduces its new system in the Dungannon shop only, then in every other shop. This is…
o: parallel changeover
phased changeover
direct changeover
pilot changeover
q.why: Whole system, one location first.

q.q: Which is a drawback of parallel changeover?
o: There is no backup if the new system fails
Staff must do every task twice, increasing cost
Only one department gets the new system
Problems affect only one section at a time
q.why: Running two systems duplicates work.

q.q: A firm switches on its new payroll module, then its invoicing module a month later. This is…
o: parallel changeover
phased changeover
direct changeover
pilot changeover
q.why: One component at a time.

q.q: Which changeover method has the highest cost?
o: Pilot
Direct
Phased
Parallel
q.why: Every transaction is processed twice.

q.q: Which changeover method is the fastest to complete?
o: Parallel
Phased
Pilot
Direct
q.why: Direct switches everyone at one moment.

q.q: Which method is the slowest to complete, according to the notes?
o: Direct
Phased
Pilot
Parallel
q.why: Phased introduces one part at a time, each working before the next.

q.q: What is the classic way to tell pilot and phased changeover apart?
o: Pilot: both systems at once. Phased: switch at one moment
Pilot: one part, everywhere. Phased: whole system, one place
Pilot: whole system, one place. Phased: one part, everywhere
Pilot: switch at one moment. Phased: both systems at once
q.why: This is the classic mix-up the notes warn against.

q.q: Sweden switched from driving on the left to the right on Dagen H in 1967. Why was this a direct changeover?
o: It was introduced in one town first
It was introduced one road at a time
Both systems ran side by side for a month
Running both systems at once was impossible
q.why: Traffic could not drive on both sides, so careful planning replaced a fallback.

q.q: Which is a drawback of pilot changeover?
o: If the system fails there is nothing to fall back on
Sharing data between sections on different systems can be difficult
Staff face all the change at one single moment
Every transaction must be processed twice everywhere
q.why: Two systems run in different sections during a pilot.

q.q: Which is a drawback of phased changeover?
o: Every job must be done twice by all staff
Old and new parts must exchange data during the changeover
The whole system goes live everywhere at once
Only one branch benefits from the system
q.why: Phased changeover takes a long time and old and new parts must share data.

q.q: A bank runs its old and new systems together for six weeks before switching off the old one. Which method is this?
o: Parallel
Direct
Pilot
Phased
q.why: Both run at the same time on the same work.

q.q: A family redecorates their house one room at a time over the summer. This is most like…
o: pilot changeover
phased changeover
direct changeover
parallel changeover
q.why: One part at a time until all is done.

q.q: Why is pilot changeover often a good balance for a supermarket chain?
o: It removes the need for any data conversion in the stores at all
Risk is limited to one store without the cost of parallel running everywhere
It avoids the need to train any of the staff in the other stores
It is always the cheapest of the four changeover methods for a chain
q.why: Problems are confined to one site and the cost is moderate.

q.q: When might direct changeover be the only realistic choice?
o: When the old and new systems cannot operate at the same time
When the new system is made of many separate modules
When failure of the new system would be catastrophic
When the organisation has many similar branches
q.why: If both cannot run together, there is no overlap option.

q.q: A hospital is introducing a new prescribing system where an error could harm patients. Which method best fits?
o: Pilot, because there is only one hospital
Direct, because it is the quickest method
Phased, because staff prefer small steps
Parallel, because the old system remains a safety net
q.why: Where failure could cause injury, parallel keeps the old system as a fallback.

q.q: A small florist with two staff and little spare time is changing system. Which method should they avoid?
o: Pilot, because it needs only one site
Parallel, because it doubles the work
Direct, because it is too slow
Phased, because the system is too small
q.why: Few staff with little spare time points away from parallel running.

q.q: What is the general rule for choosing a changeover method?
o: The method the programmers find easiest
The fastest method, whatever the cost involved
The cheapest method, whatever the level of risk
The lowest-risk method that is affordable and actually possible
q.why: Organisations seek the lowest-risk affordable and feasible method.

q.q: A new bus timetable starts on one route first, then on all the others once it works. Which method does this show?
o: Parallel
Direct
Pilot
Phased
q.why: The key feature is 'one place first'.

q.q: For full marks when recommending a changeover method, what should an answer include?
o: The method, the name of the project manager, and the date of go-live
The method, a scenario feature linked to a benefit, and why an alternative is less suitable
The method, its cost in pounds, and the length of time it will take
The method, a definition of all four methods, and a list of their advantages
q.why: Justification must use scenario facts and compare with an alternative.

q.q: A system has distinct parts – bookings, payments and reports – that can work on their own. Which method does this point towards?
o: Parallel
Pilot
Phased
Direct
q.why: Separable parts suit phased changeover.

q.q: Which best defines data conversion?
o: Deleting old records that are no longer needed
Encrypting data before sending it across a network
Backing up the data held in the system each night
Transferring existing data into the format and structure the new system requires
q.why: That is the definition.

q.q: Why is converting data from an older computer system usually quicker than from paper?
o: The data is already electronic, so it can be transferred by software
Paper records are always more accurate
No checking is ever needed on electronic data
Old computer systems hold no useful data
q.why: Software can move electronic data; paper must be keyed or scanned.

q.q: Staff type each record twice and the computer compares the two entries. This is…
o: data migration
verification
changeover
validation
q.why: Double entry checks accuracy of entry.

q.q: During data conversion, a date of 31/02 is rejected. Which process has rejected it?
o: Migration
Verification
Validation
Changeover
q.why: Validation rejects impossible values.

q.q: What is the correct order for converting data from a paper-based system?
o: Create structure, key in or scan, verify, validate
Verify, validate, create structure, key in or scan
Validate, key in or scan, verify, create structure
Key in or scan, create structure, validate, verify
q.why: The structure must exist before records can be entered and then checked.

q.q: An old system stores prices in pence; the new one needs currency in pounds. Which conversion step is needed?
o: Map codes to a lookup list
Split at the last space
Multiply by 100
Divide by 100
q.why: Pence divided by 100 gives pounds.

q.q: An old system holds a full name in one field; the new one has Forename and Surname. Which conversion step is suggested?
o: Split at the last space and check exceptions by hand
Map each name to a list of lookup codes
Copy the full name into both new fields
Split at the first space and accept every result
q.why: Splitting at the last space, with manual checks, handles most names.

q.q: What is data migration?
o: Transferring data from an older computer system to the new one
Moving staff and equipment from the old office to the new
Keying in or scanning paper records using extra staff
Running the old and new systems in parallel for a time
q.why: Migration is the computer-to-computer form of data conversion.

q.q: Why might paper data conversion need extra staff?
o: Extra staff are needed to write conversion software
The volume of records to key in or scan can be large
Paper records cannot be verified by permanent staff
The law requires independent staff to enter data
q.why: Volume can be large, especially if scanned images are stored too.

q.q: Why is computer-to-computer migration rarely a straight copy?
o: Every record must be printed and checked first
The old data must always be keyed in again by hand
Electronic data cannot be copied between systems
Fields may need reformatting and specialist conversion software
q.why: Formats often differ, e.g. dates as text or codes needing mapping.

q.q: What is the main risk of cascade training?
o: Quality may fall as knowledge is passed down each level
It needs a professional trainer at every site
It cannot be used across several sites
It is very expensive for large organisations
q.why: Each retelling can lose detail or accuracy.

q.q: Which changeover method requires all users to be fully trained before go-live?
o: Direct
Phased
Pilot
Parallel
q.why: There is no overlap period in which to learn.

q.q: Which is an advantage of e-learning?
o: Immediate face-to-face help is always available
It guarantees that staff will stay motivated
There is no cost at all to produce the materials
Staff can learn at their own pace and repeat material
q.why: Self-paced, repeatable learning is its strength.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of instructor-led classroom training?
o: Staff are away from work and the fixed pace does not suit everyone
Each person hears a different message from the trainer
There is no opportunity for hands-on practice
Questions cannot be answered until after the course
q.why: Classroom training is expensive, takes staff away and has a fixed pace.

q.q: A health trust has hundreds of shift workers across many sites. Which training approach best suits them?
o: E-learning they can complete at any time
One-to-one training for every worker
A single classroom session at head office
Manuals only, with no other support
q.why: Large numbers, many sites and shift patterns point to e-learning (or cascade).

q.q: A small office with three staff needs training on a new system. Which method suits it best?
o: A national classroom course
One-to-one, on the job
E-learning videos
Cascade training
q.why: A small office suits tailored one-to-one training.

q.q: What is the main weakness of manuals and online help as a training method?
o: They cannot be kept and used again for later reference
They are very expensive to produce and to give to each user
They are often left unread and it is hard to learn a whole system from them
They require a trainer to be present whenever they are read
q.why: Manuals are cheap and useful for reference but poor for initial training.

q.q: In a pilot changeover, how can the pilot staff help training at later sites?
o: They can write the e-learning code
They can become trainers for the next sites
They can skip training altogether
They can run the old system for other sites
q.why: Pilot staff gain experience first and can cascade it.

q.q: Which changeover method lets training be delivered one module at a time?
o: Phased
Direct
Parallel
Pilot
q.why: Phased changeover allows smaller, less stressful training steps.

q.q: Why does training help staff accept a new system?
o: Confident staff are more likely to accept change than resist it
Training removes the need for any user documentation
Trained staff will never make any data entry errors
Training means acceptance testing can be skipped
q.why: Training builds skill and confidence, which reduces resistance.

q.q: Which is NOT a reason for producing documentation at each stage?
o: To support future maintenance of the system
To remove the need for testing
To provide a starting point for the next stage
To record the work done and decisions made
q.why: Documentation supports testing; it never replaces it.

q.q: A programmer leaves halfway through a project. How does documentation help?
o: It writes the remaining code automatically
It trains the users in how to use the new system
It lets the replacement continue without reverse-engineering the code
It allows the client to cancel the contract
q.why: Continuity when personnel change is a key reason.

q.q: Which document is the main starting point for programmers?
o: User guide
Feasibility report
Post-implementation review
Design document
q.why: Programmers build from the design.

q.q: Which document is the main starting point for designers?
o: Requirements specification
Design document
Test plan
User guide
q.why: The requirements specification guides the designers.

q.q: How does documentation help resolve disputes with the client?
o: It contains the client's payment details
It lists every bug found after go-live
It removes the client's right to make changes
It records what was decided, by whom and why
q.why: A record of the work done helps resolve disputes.

q.q: Which documents are produced during the design stage?
o: Requirements specification and DFDs
Change log and post-implementation review report
Feasibility report and cost–benefit analysis
Design document, data dictionary, storyboards and initial test plan
q.why: These are the design-stage documents in the notes.

q.q: Which document is produced at the maintenance and review stage?
o: Change log
Requirements specification
Storyboards
Feasibility report
q.why: Maintenance and review produces a change log, updated technical documentation and a PIR report.

q.q: Which answer would earn the mark for 'Give a reason for producing documentation'?
o: Because documentation is useful to have
It is an aid to maintenance, so later changes are quicker and safer
So there is lots of paperwork for the project
To help people who need help with the system
q.why: Vague answers such as 'to help people' do not score.

q.q: What are the two main types of documentation for the finished system?
o: User documentation and technical documentation
Internal and external documentation
Analysis and testing documentation
Feasibility and design documentation
q.why: User documentation is for users; technical is for maintainers.

q.q: Which would be found in technical rather than user documentation?
o: A troubleshooting section
Annotated program code
Installation steps for end users
Frequently asked questions
q.why: Code listings are for programmers.

q.q: Who is the main audience for user documentation?
o: The systems analyst
The system administrator
Maintenance programmers
End users of the system
q.why: It is written for the people who use the system.

q.q: Why must technical documentation be updated after every maintenance change?
o: Otherwise it no longer matches the system and misleads future programmers
Because it is a legal requirement for all software
To train new end users in how to use the system
To increase its length so it looks more complete
q.why: Out-of-date documentation is worse than none.

q.q: Which item belongs in user documentation?
o: Server and network configuration settings
Test plans with the test data used
The data dictionary for every field
A troubleshooting guide explaining error messages
q.why: The others are technical documentation.

q.q: Which item belongs in technical documentation?
o: Training tutorials for new staff
DFDs, ER diagrams and the data dictionary
Step-by-step instructions with screenshots
Frequently asked questions for users
q.why: Data models are for those who maintain the system.

q.q: What language style is used in user documentation?
o: Plain, task-based language with screenshots
Program code listings with comments
Formal specifications and data models
Technical language with diagrams and code
q.why: User documentation is plain and task-based.

q.q: A library CalculateFine function charges juniors nothing and adults 20p per day late, capped at £5.00. What is CalculateFine(10, false)?
q.why: An adult 10 days late pays 10 × 20p = £2.00, below the cap.

q.q: Using the same library fine rules, what is CalculateFine(40, false)?
q.why: 40 × 20p = £8.00, but the fine is capped at £5.00.

q.q: Using the same library fine rules, what is CalculateFine(12, true)?
q.why: Juniors (isJunior = true) pay nothing.

q.q: What is the main benefit of good user documentation for an organisation?
o: It replaces the need for a test plan
It makes maintenance quicker and safer
It reduces help-desk calls and speeds up training
It removes the need for annotated code
q.why: Making maintenance quicker is the benefit of technical documentation.

q.q: What is system maintenance?
o: Any change applied to a system during its lifespan after it goes live
Backing up the system's data to a secure location every night
Testing the system thoroughly before handover to the client
Training new users after the system has gone live
q.why: Maintenance is any change after go-live.

q.q: Which is NOT a reason for maintenance?
o: A security hole is discovered
The system is still at the design stage
Users suggest a faster way to enter orders
The VAT rate changes
q.why: Maintenance only happens once the system is live.

q.q: Why can maintenance cost more than development over a system's life?
o: Maintenance requires new hardware every month
Maintenance programmers are always paid more
Systems are used for many years and need repeated changes
Development of systems is usually free
q.why: Many small changes over many years add up.

q.q: How does modular design reduce the cost of maintenance?
o: Each module has its own separate user guide
Modular systems never contain any errors
Changes are confined to one module, so others are unaffected
Modules never need testing after a change is made
q.why: Modular design limits the impact of each change.

q.q: How do stored test plans reduce maintenance cost?
o: They remove the need to test after changes
Tests can be re-run after each change (regression testing)
They prevent any changes being made to the code
They record which users reported each fault
q.why: Re-running stored tests checks a change has not broken anything.

q.q: Which three categories of maintenance does CCEA expect?
o: Adaptive, preventive and corrective
Corrective, preventive and perfective
Perfective, adaptive and preventive
Corrective, adaptive and perfective
q.why: Some textbooks add preventive, but CCEA expects corrective, adaptive and perfective.

q.q: The operating system on a company's servers is upgraded, and the system is changed to take advantage of it. What is this a reason for?
o: Development, because the system is not yet live
Testing, because the hardware has been replaced
Maintenance, because the infrastructure has changed
Implementation, because the old system is replaced
q.why: Infrastructure upgrades are listed as a trigger for maintenance.

q.q: Why do annotated code and meaningful identifiers reduce maintenance cost?
o: No testing is needed after changes
Users can read the code themselves
Programmers can understand the code quickly
The code runs faster on new hardware
q.why: Understanding code quickly makes changes quicker and safer.

q.q: Why can maintenance not be avoided, however well a system is designed and tested?
o: The client is legally required to request changes
Errors, business changes, laws and security threats keep arising during use
Testing always introduces new errors into the system
Systems become slower every year without maintenance
q.why: Circumstances change throughout the system's life.

q.q: A new law changes how long customer records may be kept, so the system must be altered. This is…
o: corrective maintenance
adaptive maintenance
preventive maintenance
perfective maintenance
q.why: External circumstances changed; the system was correct when built.

q.q: Adding keyboard shortcuts for experienced users is…
o: not maintenance at all
corrective maintenance
perfective maintenance
adaptive maintenance
q.why: It improves a working system.

q.q: Which type of maintenance should decrease over the life of a system?
o: Perfective
Adaptive
All three equally
Corrective
q.why: As bugs are found and fixed, fewer remain.

q.q: A large amount of adaptive maintenance soon after delivery may indicate…
o: a successful post-implementation review
excellent testing
poorly analysed user requirements
too much user training
q.why: Needs not captured in analysis surface as change requests.

q.q: Bank transfers over £65,535 are rejected by the system. What type of maintenance is needed?
o: Perfective, because transfers could be faster
Adaptive, because the business has grown
Adaptive, because banking law has changed
Corrective, because a limit in the code is wrong
q.why: 65,535 is the largest 16-bit unsigned value – a coding fault.

q.q: A second depot opens, so a depot field must be added to the system. What type of maintenance is this?
o: Corrective, because the field was missing
Adaptive, due to an external change in law
Adaptive, due to an internal change in the business
Perfective, because it improves usability
q.why: A new depot is an internal change in circumstances.

q.q: Old orders are archived so that reports load in 2 seconds rather than 9. What type of maintenance is this?
o: Perfective
Corrective
Preventive
Adaptive
q.why: It improves performance of a system that already works.

q.q: How are corrective fixes often delivered?
o: As a software patch, frequently installed automatically
As a new requirements specification
As a new feasibility study and report
As a full replacement of the system
q.why: Patches deliver corrective fixes.

q.q: Who usually pays for adaptive maintenance?
o: The developer, as it fixes a programming error
The end users through their subscriptions
The client, as the system gains new functionality
Nobody, as it is always covered by law
q.why: Adaptive maintenance adds functionality not in the original specification.

q.q: When is corrective maintenance usually carried out free by the developer?
o: When the client opens a new branch
When the law has changed
When the fault was a programming error
When users want new features
q.why: Otherwise it is covered by a maintenance contract.

q.q: Customer statements show a balance of £0.00 for some customers in error. What type of maintenance is needed?
o: Corrective
Perfective
Preventive
Adaptive
q.why: The system does not work as specified.

q.q: When does a post-implementation review take place?
o: After the system has been in use for some time
On the changeover date, as the system goes live
Before acceptance testing begins at the client
During the design stage, before any coding
q.why: Problems and benefits need time to show.

q.q: Against what is a system judged in a post-implementation review?
o: The developer's own opinion of the system
The initial test plan from the design stage
The original objectives and requirements
Competitors' similar systems on the market
q.why: Evaluation must be objective, against agreed aims.

q.q: Which is a typical output of a post-implementation review?
o: Recommendations for maintenance and lessons learned
Storyboards of the main screens and their navigation
The beta version of the software for external users
The data dictionary for each field in the system
q.why: It feeds maintenance and future projects.

q.q: What is the key difference between testing and a post-implementation review?
o: Testing asks if objectives were met after go-live; the PIR checks it works as specified before handover
Testing is carried out by users; the PIR is carried out only by programmers
Testing uses financial records; the PIR uses test data from the test plan
Testing checks it works as specified before handover; the PIR asks if objectives were met after go-live
q.why: Do not confuse the PIR with testing.

q.q: In a PIR, which evidence best shows whether predicted savings were achieved?
o: Downtime and error logs over six months
Help-desk call volumes compared with last year
Financial records compared with the feasibility forecast
Response times measured at peak hours
q.why: Cost–benefit is evaluated from financial records against the forecast.

q.q: In a PIR, which evidence best judges usability?
o: Response times and running costs
Downtime and error logs
Questionnaires and help-desk call volumes
Financial records
q.why: Usability is about whether users find it easy.

q.q: Which evaluation criterion asks 'Does it fail or lose data?'
o: Efficiency
Reliability
Effectiveness
Usability
q.why: Reliability is evidenced by downtime and error logs.

q.q: Which evaluation criterion asks 'Does it meet the requirements?'
o: Reliability
Efficiency
Usability
Effectiveness
q.why: Effectiveness uses a requirements checklist and acceptance test results.

q.q: Why does a PIR record lessons learned?
o: So the system can be signed off
So the code can be unit tested
So future projects are managed better
So the feasibility study can be repeated
q.why: Lessons learned improve future projects.

q.q: Which of these is NOT a purpose of a post-implementation review?
o: Checking whether predicted costs and benefits were achieved
Obtaining the client's sign-off at handover
Recording lessons learned for future projects
Identifying outstanding problems and recommending maintenance
q.why: Sign-off ends acceptance testing, before the PIR.
